_comment: The shared probe corpus for secret-guard.ps1 and secret_guard.py. ONE file, three consumers:
check_guard_parity.py (both guards must agree AND be right), test_secret_guard.py (the Python
twin's unit tests), and any reader who wants to know what the guard does without reading two
Written once because the alternative -- a probe list per implementation -- is how two copies
start agreeing with themselves instead of with each other. Same reason check_interpreter_parity
'expect_block' is the verdict BOTH guards must produce. A probe with expect_block=false and a
'gap' key is a KNOWN HOLE, recorded as an executable fact rather than as prose that can drift
away from the code. Those probes pass today by NOT blocking; if a future version starts
blocking one, the gate goes red and somebody has to come here and delete the gap entry, which
is exactly the moment the README should be updated too.

probes.why: A literal vendor PAT inlined into a command lands in shell history and in the transcript.
Same literal, other tool. A guard written for one tool spelling is half a guard.

probes.command: databricks secrets put-secret scope key --string-value hunter2
probes.why: --string-value puts the secret in argv. Omit it and paste at the interactive prompt.
Printing the value writes it into a transcript that persists.
The shell spelling of the same mistake.
printf is an emit verb too.
In PowerShell ($var = ...) is an expression that EMITS the assigned value.
Testing whether a secret is set reveals nothing about its value. Must stay usable.
The guard's own remediation message tells you to emit .Length instead of the value. It has to work, or the advice is unfollowable and the user reaches for the override.
The other alternative the guard's own message recommends. Same reasoning.
As .Length.
The word is not the value. Flagging prose is how a guard earns the reputation that gets it bypassed.
The explicit, intentional, greppable escape hatch. An override that must be typed is a decision; a guard with no override is one people disable wholesale.
The hook is registered for Bash|PowerShell only.
probes.gap: It therefore cannot see a secret being written INTO a file by Write/Edit. Registering it for those tools would need a different payload shape -- tool_input.content, not tool_input.command.

probes.why: The overwhelming majority of traffic. A guard that is noisy here is a guard that gets removed.

probes.gap: PIPE-TO-SHELL IS NOT COVERED. This is the headline gap and the most pointed one, because a hook is exactly the right place to catch it: permission rules split a compound on ; | && || and match each segment independently, so no deny rule can span the pipe -- but a hook sees the whole raw string. This guard is scoped to secret LEAKAGE and does not implement it.
probes.why: Recorded as an executable fact so it cannot quietly stop being true.

probes.gap: The PowerShell spelling of the same uncovered pattern.
probes.why: As above.

probes.gap: The emit-verb rule uses a 30-character proximity window to avoid firing on unrelated text on the same line. Padding past the window defeats it. Widening the window trades this hole for false positives; the window is the deliberate choice, and this is its cost.
probes.why: As above.

probes.gap: Detection is NAME-based. A secret held in a variable whose name carries none of PASSWORD/PASS/PWD/TOKEN/SECRET/APIKEY/API_KEY/CREDENTIAL is invisible to this guard.
probes.why: As above.

probes.gap: A PreToolUse hook inspects the command BEFORE it runs and never sees what it prints. A command that emits a secret without naming one cannot be caught here at all; that needs a redaction chokepoint in whatever produces the output.
probes.why: As above.
